messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Consultant
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 52

He first packs a canvas duffel and boards a cargo flight to a city that no longer appears on most maps. He is twenty-nine, a relief worker sent to distribute medical supplies through checkpoints that shift like dry earth. The war is not a headline to him; it is the smell of wet concrete and diesel, the radio static that mimics falling mortar, the weight of a child’s hand gripping his when the sirens cut through the night. He stays for eleven months. He watches supply trucks burn. He learns to sleep with his shoes on, waking at every shadow, tracking the exits, memorizing the cadence of distant fire. He tells his wife over crackling satellite calls that the work matters, that he will be fine. He never mentions the nights he scrubs his hands raw, convinced ash is still buried in his skin. When he finally returns, the silence is heavier than the bombs. At thirty-five, he takes a position as a tax consultant, trading field reports for quarterly projections. At first, the spreadsheets offer a kind of anesthesia. Numbers obey rules. Deductions balance. People are predictable. But predictability begins to fracture. He starts leaving client meetings early when the conference room fills beyond capacity. He audits the same financial line twelve times, paralyzed by the same fear of a single misplaced decimal that once kept him awake through ceasefires. He tells me he flinches when a colleague drops a stack of folders. He tells me he hasn’t sat in the back seat of a car for two years. He tells me he misses the version of himself who could look at a ledger without checking the hallway first. His marriage becomes a quiet negotiation of absence. He carries the expectations of his South Asian upbringing, where silence was often passed off as strength, a lesson he now struggles to unlearn. His wife notices how he looks through her when the television plays the news. She finds him standing on the balcony at 2 a.m., scanning the streetlights, waiting for a threat that isn’t coming. He doesn’t lie to her, but he truncates the memories. He leaves the word “war” in the doorframe. He still wakes her with a start when a car backfires. He tries to be present at dinner, but his mind splits: one half follows the conversation, the other watches the clock, calculates escape routes, rehearses what he would do if the power went out and the alarms started. He swallows the noise until it leaks out as exhaustion, guilt, and a quiet dread that he is failing them all. He comes to these sessions with a notebook full of half-finished thoughts and a quiet urgency to make sense of the fracture. He talks about the weight of being the provider, the expectation of resilience, the exhaustion of performing normalcy. He doesn’t ask for a label. He asks why his body still fights battles that ended years ago, why sleep feels like a temporary truce, why love sometimes feels like another responsibility he might break. I listen. He breathes. The room stays still.
